summary:
Haryāna stands under the national framework of India. No Haryāna-specific trans-related statute, enforcement series or documented incident pattern was identified, so a visitor's expectations in the state are set by central law and its enforcement practice.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent. If assented, the bill amends the 2019 Act to end the self-identification route to legal recognition established by the Supreme Court's 2014 judgment in NALSA v Union of India.

Under the amended scheme, legal recognition is confined to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex persons, with the wider framework otherwise recognising only male and female categories. Trans men, trans women and people who self-identify as gender-fluid or non-binary fall outside the recognition scheme. Medical certification becomes mandatory, including medical-board and district-authority certification for gender-affirming surgery.

The bill adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring people to be transgender. The People's Union for Civil Liberties has warned that these offences echo the colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. India has an estimated two million transgender people, and critics of the amendment state that the narrower definition excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid individuals.
tangentialFactors:
The bill's passage on 25 March 2026 was accompanied by protests in Mumbai, indicating organised opposition rather than a settled settlement of the issue.

The 2019 Act that the amendment revises was itself enacted in the aftermath of the 2014 NALSA judgment, which had recognised self-identification as the basis for legal gender recognition. The change therefore alters the operative standard a visitor's documents are assessed against.

No source in the inventory indicates that Haryāna applies a state-level rule on gender recognition diverging from the central scheme, nor that it operates a transgender welfare board of the kind maintained by Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha.
localsOnly:
Haryāna residents face the same certification requirement as visitors: legal recognition outside hijra, kinner and intersex categories requires medical-board and district-authority certification, and gender-affirming surgery is contingent on that certification.

Residents who self-identify as trans men, trans women, gender-fluid or non-binary have no recognised legal category under the amended scheme, which affects their standing for welfare schemes, reservations and identity documents issued in the state.

The new offences for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender, carrying up to life imprisonment, apply to conduct within the state and were opposed by the People's Union for Civil Liberties as echoing colonial-era criminalisation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The bill had not received presidential assent as of the most recent source, so its commencement date and the transitional treatment of recognition already granted under the 2019 Act remain unresolved in the available material.

No source addresses Haryāna's own implementation practice: how district authorities in the state handle certification applications, whether state police forces have revised arrest or detention procedure for trans detainees, or whether state hospitals offer gender-affirming care. These points are not sourced and are not asserted either way.

Whether the national health-coverage expansion for transition-related healthcare applied to residents of Haryāna on the same terms as elsewhere is not confirmed in this inventory.
